title: UBS resets Microsoft stock price target for investors
detail:
UBS resets Microsoft stock price target for investors
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 9:37 AM CDT 5 min read
MSFT
UBS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Not long ago, Microsoft looked like one of Big Tech's laggards. Its shares were down more than 20% for the year heading into its late July earnings report.

Then Azure grew 43%, and the stock surged 9% the next day.

Analysts are now scrambling to catch up. Ahead of the company's next report, a string of Wall Street firms, including TD Cowen, Mizuho and Citi, raised their price targets, and UBS made the biggest jump of the group.

Also read: Morgan Stanley finds a new twist in Microsoft's AI story

UBS raises Microsoft stock target from $525 to $675

UBS raised its Microsoft price target to $675 from $525 and kept a Buy rating. Analyst Karl Kierstead noted that the shares have rallied 39% since the June quarter report and returned 30% over the past six months, leaving the stock near its 52-week high.

UBS made the call ahead of the company's fiscal first-quarter report, due Oct. 28, according to Investing.com.

UBS admits the trade is getting crowded. It called Microsoft a "consensus long position," with investors now expecting more from Azure and Microsoft 365. Still, the firm said "the fundamentals support those higher expectations" and argued the stock's valuation at 23 times calendar 2027 earnings "is not stretched."

Azure is doing the heavy lifting. The cloud business grew 43% in the June quarter and crossed $100 billion in annualized revenue, and management guided for about 45% growth in the September quarter. Revenue in the broader Intelligent Cloud segment rose 32% to $39.3 billion, as reported by TheStreet.

Demand is still running ahead of supply. Microsoft said "customer demand for Azure remained higher than available capacity," while its commercial backlog jumped 84% to $678 billion.

Excluding OpenAI, that backlog still grew 25%, and Microsoft 365 Copilot now has well over 30 million paid seats.

UBS raised its Microsoft price target to $675 from $525 and kept a Buy rating.Bloomberg / Getty Images
UBS is not alone in bullish Microsoft view

Other firms are lining up behind the same story.

TD Cowen raised its target to $625 from $540 and sees the potential for a "higher than normal" Azure beat, pointing to third-party data that screened as the strongest in history, a full quarter of its Fairwater data center, and a bullish read on OpenAI's growth.

The upgrades kept coming from there. Mizuho lifted its target to $600 from $510 after channel checks it called "very healthy overall," while Citi raised its target to $636 from $600, citing survey and reseller checks that point to faster growth in productivity software and public cloud. Citi also ranks Microsoft among the best-positioned AI vendors.

title: Here's How Microsoft's $175 Billion in Capital Expenditures Is Hurting Its Business
detail:
Here's How Microsoft's $175 Billion in Capital Expenditures Is Hurting Its Business
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

MSFT
NVDA
OPAI.PVT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) is among the big three cloud computing infrastructure providers and is always included in any list of AI hyperscalers. It's heavily pursuing a massive amount of AI computing power for its internal service, Copilot, while also powering other products like OpenAI's ChatGPT through its cloud computing platform, Azure.

To support this growth, Microsoft is investing heavily in data centers. This year alone, it expects its capital expenditures to hit $175 billion, with most of that going toward constructing and equipping data centers. That is leading to strong growth, but what if this growth is actually hurting its business?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

While it may sound odd, Microsoft's business is actually being harmed by the heavy pursuit of its cloud computing empire. Here's why.

Image source: Getty Images.
Microsoft is spending big

At first, you may imagine that the reason that these capital expenditures are hurting Microsoft is that it could be spending that $175 billion in ways that generate a more direct return for shareholders, such as on share buybacks or dividends. But that's not what I'm talking about. In fact, I'm OK with Microsoft spending big on AI because it needs to evolve its business to adapt to the AI age or risk being left behind.

Moreover, Microsoft's spending is resulting in strong growth. Azure saw its revenue rise 43% during its latest quarter, passing a $100 billion annual run rate. Additionally, Copilot reached 30 million paid seats, indicating strong adoption of the proprietary AI platform. Overall, Microsoft's revenue rose 18% last quarter.

While that's impressive for a company that's as large as Microsoft, there's a major caveat.

Azure's operating margin likely isn't as good as the rest of Microsoft's business

Unfortunately for investors, Microsoft doesn't publicly break out detailed statistics for its individual segments, such as Azure's operating margins. However, Azure's chief competitors, Amazon Web Services (AWS) (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Google Cloud from Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), freely share that information. It's unlikely that Microsoft Azure's margins are much different from theirs, since they operate using essentially the same business model. During the most recent quarter, Google Cloud's operating margin was 36% while AWS' was 39%. So, I think it's highly likely that Azure's operating margins are in the high-30% range.

Railroads transformed America and fiber optic cable built the internet, yet many investors who funded both lost money. In a note reported on October 16, 2026, Bank of America investment strategist Sebastian Raedler argued AI is tracking the same path, writing that "most major capital cycles of the past have ended in disappointment, even though the underlying technology often lived up to expectations."

24/7 Wall St.

Raedler argues that AI's technology can succeed while investors in AI stocks still earn poor returns. Sebastian Raedler said 12-month forward consensus hyperscaler capex expectations rose from $330 billion in early 2025 to $1 trillion. Those figures forecast spending by the largest cloud operators over the next year.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 2.5%, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index posted its eighth straight loss, its longest run since 2008. After Bank of America's note, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) slid 1.43% to $214.13, a market value of $5.17 trillion. On Raedler's warning, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) fell 1.93% to $529.05, and its market value slipped below $4 trillion to $3.93 trillion.

How Capital Cycles Punish Investors

In a capital cycle, strong profits pull in a wave of investment until capacity exceeds demand. Prices then fall as competitors fight for customers, and returns on capital sink.

title: Why You Should Think About Palantir Differently Now
detail:
Why You Should Think About Palantir Differently Now
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock trades at 78.2 times sales, compared to 3.1 for the S&P 500. Investors paying that premium need to know exactly what they are buying, and the case Palantir makes has evolved. During the fiscal Q3 2024 earnings call, executives highlighted the fast-growing number of U.S. businesses signing on as customers. By the latest call in fiscal Q2 2026, the focus had shifted. So what does management talk up now?

Palantir Now Makes The Case For Sovereign AI

By sovereign AI, Palantir means an architecture where companies maintain full control over their own data and the artificial intelligence built upon it. During the fiscal Q2 2026 call, held August 3, 2026, executives reported immense demand from enterprises for this capability. They contrasted this approach with purchasing external services from AI labs, a process they described as paying outside vendors to move proprietary corporate knowledge into third-party models.

The pitch sounded quite different during the fiscal Q3 2024 call. At that time, leadership highlighted that Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count grew to 321. Expanding that baseline served as a clear signal that more U.S. companies were adopting the software.

While Palantir still reports the customer count, the metric no longer takes center stage. Instead, the company links sovereign AI directly to increased spending per client. Customers that previously utilized only the Foundry software now want access to the broader sovereign AI stack. The core argument now rests on the size of individual customer commitments, rather than the sheer number of clients.

Shifts like this test every retirement plan. If your advisor recently retired, it is a good moment for a free second opinion from our partner firm.

Palantir's Business Customers Are Spending Much Larger Sums

Sales to the U.S. businesses are growing much faster than the number of businesses buying. Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count reached 653 in fiscal Q2 2026, up 35% from a year earlier. Over that same period, U.S. commercial revenue rose 149% to $764 million. These buyers belong to Palantir's commercial segment, a division that generated $2.07 billion in fiscal 2025, accounting for 46.3% of the company's total revenue that year.

Contract values follow a similar trajectory. U.S. businesses signed deals with Palantir worth $2.132 billion in total in fiscal Q2 2026, up 153% from a year earlier. Consequently, the average customer is committing significantly more capital than they were just a year ago. Executives labeled that contract total a record, forming the foundation of the case they now present.

title: Not Alphabet. Not Microsoft. This Is the Cloud Stock I'd Buy With $5,000 Right Now.

Not Alphabet. Not Microsoft. This Is the Cloud Stock I'd Buy With $5,000 Right Now.

When investors think about cloud computing, Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL)(NASDAQ: GOOG) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) are often the first names that come to mind. But Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) is also making a strong push into AI infrastructure, and its rapidly growing cloud business offers another way to ride the AI boom.

With $5,000 to put to work today, investors may find Oracle a more compelling cloud choice than either of those giants. The reason starts with how fast its cloud business is growing.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
This database giant is becoming a major force in AI cloud

Oracle may be best known for its database software, which businesses use to store and manage critical information. These days, that established business is laying the foundation for a much bigger opportunity: supplying the cloud infrastructure that other companies need to develop and run AI models.

Oracle's cloud infrastructure business is already seeing solid growth, with revenue climbing 121% to $7.4 billion in its most recent quarter. That suggests its cloud business is becoming an important growth engine rather than simply an extension of its traditional software business.

Its massive backlog, meanwhile, provides a longer runway for growth. Oracle's remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached a record $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year. RPO represents contracted revenue that has not yet been recognized, giving investors a clearer view of the company's future revenue.

That means Oracle is seeing surging demand from customers that need cloud capacity for AI training, applications, and inference. Still, that demand isn't limited to one type of customer, and Oracle is positioning itself to capture several parts of that market.

But with competition picking up, the next question is how Oracle is setting itself apart from the biggest names in the cloud business.

Oracle has a different advantage from its larger cloud rivals

Microsoft Azure and Alphabet's Google Cloud compete across broad cloud ecosystems. However, Oracle's opportunity is somewhat different: it has the luxury of combining its established database business with cloud infrastructure designed for demanding enterprise workflows.

That matters because companies wouldn't want to rebuild their IT systems every time a new AI model arrives. Oracle's database expertise helps here, allowing companies to integrate AI into the systems and data they already rely on without disrupting operations.

Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), a consumer electronics and personal computing hardware provider, closed at $343.46, up 0.43%. The stock edged higher after reports that iPhone Duo preorders sold out quickly, and investors are watching the November 2 earnings call for guidance and demand updates.

Trading volume reached 59 million shares, coming in about 31% above its three-month average of 45 million shares.

How the markets moved today

S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) closed at 7,659, down 1.09%, while Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) finished at 26,140, down 2.14%. Among consumer electronics and personal computing hardware peers, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) closed at $529.05, down 1.93%, and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) closed at $340.59, down 2.47%, as investors kept focus on AI-debt pressure and semiconductor weakness.

What this means for investors

Apple shares rose on Friday, Oct. 16, when pre-orders for its new iPhone Duo sold out within minutes in the morning. The Duo is the company's first foldable smartphone. It includes a 5.4-inch front display with a 7.6-inch foldable inner screen. Delivery dates quickly shifted from Oct. 23 into late January.

The strong demand for Apple's latest device propelled its stock back toward the 52-week high of $348.15 reached earlier in the week. In the company's 2026 third quarter, ended June 27, Apple posted record performance as revenue reached $109.4 billion, which represented a 16% year-over-year increase. The iPhone maker beat Wall Street expectations on revenue and profit, but investors focused on strong iPhone 17 demand and a softer near-term outlook that later weighed on sentiment.

With the Duo's preliminary success, Apple could see strong 2027 sales results. The question is how much of a headwind macroeconomic conditions, such as persistent inflation and rising interest rates, will be for the tech giant.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

(Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The Nasdaq Composite plunged Friday, halting its four-week rally, amid a technology sell-off on Wall Street.

The index declined 2.1% to 26,140.03. The S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659.44, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.3% to 52,002.41.

Among sectors, tech led the laggards, while energy paced the gainers.

This week, the Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, ending its four-week winning streak. That weekly performance marked the worst since June.

The S&P 500 ended the week down 1.9% and the Dow gained 0.7%.

Alphabet (GOOGL), Salesforce (CRM), Cisco Systems (CSCO), Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN), and Nvidia (NVDA) were the biggest decliners on the Dow.

Micron Technology (MU), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Sandisk (SNDK) also fell.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite hit fresh closing highs Oct. 6, but the rally had been powered by only a few tech giants, suggesting underlying weakness on Wall Street.

Many analysts fear a potential stock market correction as the majority of S&P 500 stocks have been hovering well below all-time highs.

Treasury yields were mixed. The two-year rate fell 3.2 basis points at 4.72%, while the 10-year rate was unchanged at 5.09%.

US industrial production grew more than expected in September as manufacturing output rebounded despite weakness in the auto component, Federal Reserve data showed.

Brent crude jumped 3.4% to $109.53 a barrel in Friday late-afternoon trade, while West Texas Intermediate was 3.8% higher at $101.64. Both benchmarks were up for the week, with Brent on track for its fourth consecutive weekly increase.

Saudi Arabia intercepted multiple missiles and drones on Friday, including a missile heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, CNBC reported, citing a military spokesperson.

US lawmakers introduced a bill Friday to block President Donald Trump's deal to allow export of hundreds of millions of barrels of Russian diesel, Bloomberg News reported.

Spot gold fell 0.1% to $4,166.56 per troy ounce, while silver remained steady at $57.14 per ounce.
